caption: "converse ad" — 100,000+ searches this week. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the 118-year-old company in the news.

Why: on September 19 Converse pulled an Instagram ad of K-pop star Karina holding Chuck 70 X sneakers after critics said the image evoked Ku Klux Klan and lynching imagery. Converse said it "got this wrong" and removed it.

What most people don't know: Nike has owned Converse since 2003, bought for $309 million out of bankruptcy. In the 1960s about 90% of pro and college basketball players wore its shoes, and by 2000 it had sold more than 600 million pairs of All Stars.
Very simply put: a 1917 basketball shoe, owned by its rival since 2003.

slides.headline: The ad: K-pop star Karina holding *Chuck 70 X* sneakers.
slides.sub: Posted on Instagram. Critics said the image evoked Ku Klux Klan and lynching imagery. Converse apologized on September 19 and removed it.
slides.image: A smartphone lying face down on a white table beside a pair of black canvas sneakers, phone in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain white, photorealistic, no logos, no text

slides.headline: Founded *February 1908* in Malden, Massachusetts.
slides.sub: By Marquis Mills Converse. The All Star basketball shoe arrived in 1917.
slides.image: A red brick New England factory building with tall windows under a clear sky, building in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain empty street, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: Chuck Taylor joined as a *salesman* in the early 1920s.
slides.sub: His suggestions reshaped the shoe within a year. His signature went on the ankle patch in 1932.
slides.image: A vintage leather suitcase and a fedora on a wooden train platform bench, suitcase in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wooden planks, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: In the 1960s, *90%* of basketball players wore them.
slides.sub: Pro and college. Converse held 70 to 80 percent of the basketball shoe market.
slides.image: An old wooden basketball court with a leather ball at the free-throw line, hoop in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain polished floor, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: Official Olympic shoe from *1936 to 1968*.
slides.sub: And the US armed forces' training shoe in World War Two.
slides.image: A vintage cinder running track with white lane lines in morning light, track in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain infield grass, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: More than *600 million* pairs of All Stars by 2000.
slides.sub: Then bankruptcy on January 22, 2001. It was the company's second, after 1929.
slides.image: Hundreds of canvas sneakers in mixed colours piled in a warehouse bin, shoes in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain concrete floor, photorealistic, no logos, no text

slides.headline: Nike bought it out of bankruptcy for *$309 million*.
slides.sub: July 2003. Production moved to China, India, Vietnam and Indonesia. Revenue in 2023: $2.4 billion.
slides.image: Rows of sewing machines in a bright shoe factory, machines in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain grey floor, photorealistic, no people, no logos, no text

slides.headline: The Chuck 70 is a *2013* reissue of the 1970 shoe.
slides.sub: Thicker canvas, higher midsole, one-piece rubber sole. The All Star has appeared in more than 650 films.
slides.image: A single black canvas high-top sneaker on a white pedestal under gallery lighting, shoe in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain white, photorealistic, no logos, no text

slides.headline: Very simply put: a 1917 basketball shoe, *owned by Nike* since 2003.
